title: Pleasure, danger, escape
hookLine: the gratification, the danger and the way out of sense pleasure (MN 13)
carry: the escape is from the hook

cards: Every app store page has the same layout. What it does. The screenshots.
Five-star reviews from people who love it. Almost none has a section called: what this will cost you. And none has a third: how to stop using it when you want to.
MN 13 asks for all three, about sense pleasure. Not to ruin the pleasure. To see the whole of it, plainly, before deciding.

teach.b: MN 13, the Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering, looks at sense pleasure three ways.

The gratification, the danger, the escape. Gratification first, and the Buddha doesn't deny it. The pleasure and joy that arise from the five cords of sense pleasure, sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches, are real.

Then the danger. A person earns a living by a trade: counting, accounting, farming, trading, herding, archery, service to the king. They face cold and heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, hunger and thirst.
If the work fails, they grieve: all my effort was for nothing. If it succeeds, they worry: kings, thieves, fire or flood could take it, or an heir could squander it.

And the larger danger: for the sake of pleasures, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, householders with householders; mother with son, son with mother, brother with sister, friend with friend.
Then the escape: the removal of desire and lust for sense pleasures. Not the removal of every joy. In MN 36, the Buddha says he came to see that the joy of deep meditation wasn't something to fear.
The escape is from the hook, not from happiness.
The sutta says anyone who doesn't see gratification as gratification, danger as danger and escape as escape can't fully understand sense pleasures, let alone guide someone else.
And he applies the same three to the body and to feelings.

how: Buddhist teachers use the triad of gratification, danger and escape as a way of reflecting on desires; the lay precepts ask for restraint in sense pleasures rather than renouncing them.

o: something to avoid entirely on the spiritual path
a sin that always needs to be confessed
something real, seen with its danger and its way out

games.q: match the three, and the danger.
p: quarrel for the sake of pleasures

s: MN 13 denies that sense pleasures are pleasant
it names the gratification first, as real.
in MN 36, the Buddha says the joy of deep meditation isn't something to fear
the escape is from the hook, not from happiness.
MN 13 says even successful work brings danger
worry that kings, thieves, fire or flood will take what was earned.

games.q: a person's business succeeds. in MN 13, what comes with the success?
o: worry that kings, thieves, fire or flood will take it
games.why: success brings its own danger: guarding what you have. the sutta follows pleasure all the way to quarrels between families and kings.

practice: Think of one pleasure you love, coffee, a show, a certain food, and give it its due: notice the real enjoyment in it, even in memory. Then name its cost plainly, without shame, in time, money, sleep or peace.
Last, touch the third lightly: what would it be like to enjoy it without needing it? Nothing has to be given up; just see all three.

wordCard.voice: Pleasure. In MN 13, sense pleasure is seen three ways: its gratification, its danger, and the way out.

orig.note: Pali nissaraṇa: escape, the way out; the third of the triad.

carryVoice: Your line: the escape is from the hook. The joy itself can stay. Day four hundred eleven.
